text: menstrual cases.4 Treatment of the acute phase re- quires prevention of further production or absorption of toxin by local measures such as removal of tampons or packing, wound debridement, or drainage of abscesses; elimination of the toxin-producing bacteria by antistaphy- lococcal antibacterials given intravenously initially; fluid replacement; and sometimes corticosteroids.1,2 Drotrec- ogin alfa has also been tried.5 Continuing antibacterial treatment for 10 days during the convalescent phase to re- duce the risk of recurrence has been recommended.1 The use of prophylactic antibacterial therapy has been suggest- ed in burns patients,6 but this is controversial. Group A beta-haemolytic streptococci (Streptococcus py- ogenes) have been associated with a similar toxin-related syndrome.7,8 Benzylpenicillin is the treatment of choice9 but, since it may be difficult to exclude staphylococcal tox- ic shock syndrome, an antistaphylococcal drug such as flu- cloxacillin should also be given.9 Clinical improvement has been reported with intravenous normal immunoglobu- lins.10,11 Toxic shock syndromes may be associated with necrotis- ing fasciitis (see p.180). 1.
